newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Beijing vows strict control over market surge.
newsitem.headline: Beijing vows strict control over market surge.

text.p: China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong has vowed further action to cool speculation in the country's heated stock markets and punish officials guilty of improper conduct, a newspaper reported on Tuesday.
"We will work hard to put the stock market in order to serve the interests of the national economy," Dai, governor of the People's Bank of China, told the South China Morning Post.
"When the market grows too rapidly, it becomes a bubble market. Relevant departments will take measures to regularise the markets," he was quoted by the newspaper as saying.
While Dai did not specify what further action would be taken to put a brake on speculation, he singled out banks as a prime source for hot money entering local markets.
"We have banned banks from investing in stocks...we have imposed punishments and fines on those who act illegally in the stock market," Dai was quoted as saying.
Dai reaffirmed that Hong Kong would enjoy fiscal autonomy after it returns to China on July 1, but said that help from Beijing would be close at hand, if the territory wanted it.

"We will provide support. This is the case not only with Hong Kong but we have similar arrangements with other central banks, for example with Thailand, to maintain currency stability in the region," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
Dai also suggested that Hong Kong's huge foreign reserves and Land Fund, estimated at HK$150 billion, could be used to stabilise the Hong Kong dollar, if that was necessary.
Hong Kong's foreign reserves stood at US$63.6 billion at end-April.

Hong Kong, a British colony of over 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight June 30. Under Sino-British treaties on Hong Kong's handover, it is promised a high degree of self rule for a further 50 years, including fiscal independence and maintenance of a separate currency.
